title: Psalm 145: Your Kingdom Is an Everlasting Kingdom
summary: David vows to exalt and bless God as King every day and forever. He praises the LORD's unsearchable greatness, his mighty acts told from generation to generation, his grace, compassion, and loving devotion, and his everlasting kingdom. The LORD upholds all who fall, feeds every living thing, is near to all who call on him in truth, and preserves all who love him. The psalm ends by calling every creature to bless his holy name.
story: Psalm 145 is the last psalm in the Psalter attributed to David, and it forms the climax of the final Davidic collection (Psalms 138 to 145). After the struggles of Psalms 140 to 143 and the royal hope of Psalm 144, David the king now praises God as the true King whose kingdom is everlasting. The psalm ends with a call for every creature to bless God's holy name, and the Psalter answers in the next five psalms (146 to 150), each beginning and ending with Hallelujah. Psalm 145 is the doorway to that final crescendo of praise.
historical:
The heading reads “A Psalm of praise. Of David.” It is the only psalm whose heading uses the word tehillah, praise, the singular of Tehillim, the Hebrew name of the whole book of Psalms. As with other headings, scholars debate whether “Of David” names the author or marks a collection. Many scholars date the psalm after the exile because of its acrostic form and some features of its vocabulary; others accept a Davidic origin.

The psalm is an acrostic: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In the traditional Hebrew text (the Masoretic Text), the verse for the letter nun is missing, leaving twenty-one verses for the twenty-two letters. The great Psalms Scroll found among the Dead Sea Scrolls in Cave 11 at Qumran (11QPsa) and the Septuagint both include a nun line, which the BSB and many modern translations include as the second half of verse 13: “The LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions.” Many scholars think this line is original and dropped out of the Masoretic tradition by accident, though some think it was added later to complete the pattern.

In Jewish tradition Psalm 145, known as Ashrei (from the word for blessed with which it is introduced in the prayer book, drawn from Psalm 84:4 and 144:15), is recited three times daily. The Talmud (Berakhot 4b) singles it out for special honor.
cultural:
The acrostic form served several purposes in the ancient world. It aided memory, made the psalm easy to learn and recite, and conveyed completeness: God is praised from A to Z, with nothing left out. The same form is found in Psalms 111, 112, 119, and in Lamentations 1 to 4.

The psalm's picture of God as King drew on the royal ideals of the ancient Near East. Kings were expected to defend the weak, feed the hungry, and uphold justice. Psalm 145 attributes all these duties to the LORD and more: he upholds all who fall, lifts those bowed down, and gives every creature its food in season. The reference to food in its season (verse 15) reflects an agricultural world dependent on the timing of rain and harvest, where God's provision was experienced as the right weather at the right time.
literary: Psalm 145 is a hymn of praise built as an alphabetic acrostic. Its structure is framed by the psalmist's personal vow to praise (verses 1 and 2) and his final declaration (verse 21), which widens to every creature. Between these, the psalm moves through God's greatness (verses 3 to 7), his grace and goodness (verses 8 to 10), his kingdom (verses 11 to 13), and his care for all who depend on him (verses 14 to 20). Verse 8 quotes the great self-description God gave Moses at Sinai (Exodus 34:6), gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion. The word all appears repeatedly, especially in verses 13 to 21, stressing that God's care and kingdom reach everyone and everything. The kingdom verses (11 to 13) sit at the center of the acrostic, where the letters kaph, lamed, and mem form (in reverse order) the Hebrew word for king, a pattern many scholars think is deliberate.

outline.t: I will exalt you, my God and King
Great is the LORD: his works told across generations
Gracious and compassionate, good to all
The glory of his everlasting kingdom
Near to all who call, upholding all who fall
Let every creature bless his holy name

doctrines.note: God is King, and his kingdom is everlasting, enduring through all generations. The psalm describes that kingdom not as mere power but as faithfulness, kindness, provision, and nearness to all who call on him.

The psalm quotes God's self-revelation to Moses: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. It adds his greatness, righteousness, goodness to all, and nearness to all who call on him.
The eyes of all look to God, and he gives them food in season; he opens his hand and satisfies every living thing. Every creature depends on God's daily care.

words.note: Malkut, kingdom or royalty. The word describes royal rule and the realm over which a king reigns. It appears four times in verses 11 to 13, the center of the psalm. God's kingdom is glorious, everlasting, and enduring through all generations, unlike the kingdoms of human rulers.

Channun, gracious. The word describes favor freely given, kindness shown to those who have no claim on it. In the Old Testament it is used almost only of God. Verse 8 draws it from Exodus 34:6, the passage where God proclaimed his own name and character to Moses.

Qarov, near. The word describes closeness in space, time, or relationship. Verse 18 says the LORD is near to all who call on him in truth. The God whose greatness is unsearchable (verse 3) is also near, available to any who call on him honestly.

Chasid, faithful one or saint. The word is related to chesed, loving devotion, and describes those who live in covenant loyalty to God. In verse 10 the saints bless God. They are people shaped by the loving devotion they have received.

christ: Psalm 145 celebrates God's everlasting kingdom, and the New Testament proclaims that this kingdom has come near in Jesus. Jesus began his ministry announcing that the kingdom of God is at hand (Mark 1:15). The psalm's description of God upholding those who fall, lifting up those bowed down, and feeding the hungry is lived out in Jesus' ministry, who healed a woman bent over for eighteen years (Luke 13:10-13) and fed crowds in the wilderness (Mark 6:30-44). The God who is near to all who call on him became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The psalm's vision of every creature blessing God's holy name finds its fulfillment in Revelation 5:13, where every creature in heaven and on earth gives praise to the one on the throne and to the Lamb. The link is both thematic and theological: the King the psalm praises has come in person.
questions: The psalm says God's greatness is unsearchable and that he is near to all who call on him. How do you hold together God's greatness and his nearness?
Verse 4 speaks of one generation commending God's works to the next. What have you received from an older generation, and what are you passing on?
The psalm says God upholds all who fall and lifts those bowed down. Who do you know who needs that kind of lifting, and how might you be part of it?
